synthesis.title: Evidence-based typography for sustained digital reading
synthesis.note: Bootstrapped from a secondary synthesis (research cutoff 11 Nov 2026) available only as a text summary with about 30 linked sources; the full 44-reference report was not available. All summaries in this registry are original wording. W3C documents and a subset of primary studies were checked against originals on 2026-11-12 (see evidence/VERIFICATION.md); everything else is marked unverified-secondary. Normative, empirical, heuristic and hypothesis claims are kept distinct, and claims that lack a reliable quantitative improvement say so explicitly.

sources.title: Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2

review.notes: Fetched 2026-11-12. Version REC-WCAG22-20241212 (W3C Recommendation, 12 December 2024). Levels and requirement summaries for the listed criteria confirmed. The fetch tool processed the first ~100k characters of the page; all listed criteria appeared in that portion.

sources.title: Understanding Success Criterion 1.4.3: Contrast (Minimum)

review.locator: Success criterion text; large-scale text definition and point-to-pixel note
review.notes: Fetched 2026-11-12 (page shows 'Updated 04 October 2026'). Confirmed: AA; 4.5:1 for text; 3:1 for large-scale text; large scale = at least 18pt or 14pt bold (or CJK equivalent); 1pt = 1.333px so roughly 24px and 18.5px. Minor rounding difference: the synthesis says 14pt bold is about 18.7px; W3C says about 18.5px (14 x 1.333 = 18.66). The Understanding document is informative; the normative text is in S-wcag22.

sources.title: Understanding Success Criterion 1.4.6: Contrast (Enhanced)

review.locator: Success criterion text and intent section
review.notes: Fetched 2026-11-12. Confirmed: AAA; 7:1 for text; 4.5:1 for large-scale text; thresholds are not rounded (4.499:1 fails 4.5:1); size is judged as delivered, before user resizing; very thin fonts may need more contrast than the ratio implies.

sources.title: Understanding Success Criterion 1.4.12: Text Spacing

review.locator: Success criterion text; intent section on author obligations
review.notes: Fetched 2026-11-12. Confirmed: AA; no loss of content or functionality when users set line height >= 1.5x, paragraph spacing >= 2x, letter spacing >= 0.12x, word spacing >= 0.16x font size; exception for scripts that do not use a property; authors need not use these values or provide a mechanism to set them.

sources.title: Understanding Success Criterion 1.4.10: Reflow

review.locator: Success criterion text; intent section on 400% zoom
review.notes: Fetched 2026-11-12. Confirmed: AA; no two-dimensional scrolling at 320 CSS px width (vertically scrolling content) or 256 CSS px height (horizontally scrolling content); equivalent to 1280px at 400% zoom; exceptions for content needing two-dimensional layout (maps, diagrams, video, games, presentations, data tables, toolbars).

sources.title: Understanding Success Criterion 1.4.4: Resize Text

review.notes: Fetched 2026-11-12. Confirmed: AA; text can be resized up to 200% without assistive technology and without loss of content or functionality; captions and images of text excepted.

sources.title: Understanding Success Criterion 1.4.8: Visual Presentation

review.notes: Fetched 2026-11-12. Confirmed: AAA; a mechanism (which may be the user agent) is available so that users can select foreground/background colours; width is no more than 80 characters or glyphs (40 if CJK); text is not justified; line spacing is at least space-and-a-half within paragraphs and paragraph spacing at least 1.5 times the line spacing; text can be resized to 200% without assistive technology and without horizontal scrolling to read a line on a full-screen window.

sources.title: W3C Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 3.0 — W3C Working Draft

review.locator: Status section; 'Text contrast sufficient (minimum)' and '(enhanced)' requirements and editor's notes
review.notes: Fetched 2026-11-12 (WebFetch summary plus full-page text search). This version: https://www.w3.org/TR/2026/WD-wcag-3.0-20260910/ (Working Draft, 10 September 2026), matching the synthesis. The text contrast requirements read '@@[contrast measure to be determined]' with status 'Developing', and an editor's note says the WCAG 3 contrast algorithm is yet to be determined. The strings 'APCA' and 'Advanced Perceptual' do not occur anywhere in the page. The document states that WCAG 3 does not replace WCAG 2. Status is 'verified-normative' only in the sense that the W3C document itself was checked; a Working Draft is not a normative standard.

sources.title: The Effects of Line Length on Reading Performance of Online News Articles
sources.venue: Proceedings of the Human Factors and Ergonomics Society Annual Meeting 49(5):701-705

review.notes: DOI resolves to SAGE (landing page returned HTTP 403 to automated fetch). Bibliographic data and abstract obtained from Crossref (publisher-deposited). Abstract confirms 20 college-age students; 35/55/75/95 CPL; fastest reading at 95 CPL; satisfaction unaffected; strong preference for the extreme line lengths. Detailed numbers were checked in the companion Usability News article (S-shaikh-2005-usability-news).

sources.title: The Effects of Line Length on Reading Online News
sources.venue: Usability News 7.2 (Software Usability Research Laboratory; archived on the RUX blog)

review.notes: Fetched 2026-11-12. Confirmed: 20 college-age students; Arial 10pt with 12pt interlinear spacing; mean WPM 167.21 / 167.38 / 169.44 / 178.82 at 35 / 55 / 75 / 95 CPL; F(3,57)=3.45, p=.02, eta^2=.15; no effect on overall comprehension; reading efficiency marginal (p=.06); no satisfaction or preference main effect, but all participants named an extreme length (35 or 95 CPL) as most and least preferred. The 6.8% figure in the synthesis is derived (178.82/167.38) and is not stated in the article. The page lists A. Dawn Shaikh as author; the HFES paper adds Chaparro.

sources.title: The influence of reading speed and line length on the effectiveness of reading from screen

review.notes: NOT VERIFIED. DOI identified via Crossref bibliographic search (title, authors, journal, volume, pages match). The ScienceDirect page returned HTTP 403 and Crossref holds no abstract (it confirms authors Mary C. Dyson and Mark Haselgrove), so none of the study details (n=36, 55 vs 100 CPL comprehension, p<.05) were checked. sources.title: The Effects of Line Length and Method of Movement on Patterns of Reading from Screen

review.notes: Fetched 2026-11-12. This is the page the synthesis linked for Dyson & Haselgrove (2001); it is in fact Dyson & Kipping (1998). Abstract confirms: 25, 55 and 100 CPL; long lines (100) read faster than very short lines (25); comprehension similar; readers rated 55 CPL easiest and 100 CPL hardest; scrolling patterns affected reading rate. Sample sizes (48 and 24 per the synthesis) are not stated on the landing page and were not checked. No DOI shown.

sources.title: The Effects of Line Length on Children and Adults' Online Reading Performance
sources.venue: Usability News 4.2 (Software Usability Research Laboratory; archived on the RUX blog)

review.notes: Fetched 2026-11-12. Confirmed: 20 adults and 20 children; ~45 / 76 / 132 CPL (330 / 550 / 930 px); 12pt Arial black on white; 17-inch 1024x768 96 dpi monitor; adult reading times 366 / 363 / 370 s (narrow / medium / full), p=.88; children 266 / 279 / 276 s, p=.40; adults preferred the medium length, children the narrow length; both ranked full-screen last. DISCREPANCY: the synthesis dates the study 2003; the linked article is Usability News 4.2, posted 11 July 2002. A 2003 conference version may exist but was not checked.

sources.title: Readability: The Optimal Line Length

review.notes: Fetched 2026-11-12. Confirmed: recommends 50-75 characters per line; evidence is qualitative observation from Baymard's e-commerce usability testing plus Emil Ruder's typography guidance and WCAG 1.4.8. No measured reading-speed effect is reported, and 65 CPL / an 80->65 change is not mentioned.

sources.title: Make It Big! The Effect of Font Size and Line Spacing on Online Readability
sources.venue: Proceedings of the 2016 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems, pp. 3637-3648

review.locator: Design, Equipment, Results (fixation duration and comprehension by font size and line spacing; Table 2)
review.notes: DOI resolves to the ACM DL (HTTP 403 to automated fetch); Crossref metadata confirmed; full text read from the author PDF at https://www.pielot.org/pubs/Rello2016-Fontsize.pdf. Confirmed: 104 participants, 93 analysed; Tobii 1750, 17-inch 1024x768, ~60 cm; Arial; sizes 10/12/14/18/22/26 pt; spacing 0.8/1.0/1.4/1.8 where 1.0 is Firefox's default equal to 120% of font size (so 0.96/1.20/1.68/2.16 font-relative, as the synthesis says); spacing effect on fixation duration F(3,89)=0.064, p=.978; mean fixation duration .224 s at 14pt and .208 s at 18pt; font-size effect F(5,445)=66.825, p<.001. OMISSIONS IN THE SYNTHESIS: (1) line spacing significantly affected comprehension (Kruskal-Wallis chi^2(3)=19.56, p<.001): the smallest spacing (0.8) scored lower than 1.0, 1.4 and 1.8; (2) comprehension was lower at 10 and 12 pt than at 18 pt. The full title shown here was taken from the PDF; Crossref lists only 'Make It Big!'.

sources.title: The role of visual crowding in eye movements during reading: Effects of text spacing

review.notes: DOI resolves to Springer (login redirect for automated fetch); full text read via Europe PMC (PMC10600290, CC BY). Confirmed: 36 participants; four-line passages; 19-point Inconsolata; 20-inch monitor at 65 cm; first-fixation duration 232.31 / 230.11 / 227.74 ms (condensed / standard / wide); wide-vs-standard FFD p=.032 and total viewing time p=.187; undersweep rate 36.48% (condensed) vs 39.78% (standard), standard-vs-condensed p=.01. Note: total viewing time (TVT) is a word-level eye-movement measure (309.17 vs 305.55 ms), not whole-passage reading time.

sources.title: Does print size matter for reading? A review of findings from vision science and typography

review.notes: The author-hosted PDF linked by the synthesis returned HTTP 403. DOI identified via Crossref; abstract read via Europe PMC (PMID 21828237, PMC3428264). Confirmed: fluent range of print size spans about a factor of 10, from roughly 0.2 to 2 degrees of x-height; at 40 cm that corresponds to about 1.4 mm (4 pt) to 14 mm (40 pt). Full text not read.

sources.title: Towards Individuated Reading Experiences: Different Fonts Increase Reading Speed for Different Individuals
sources.venue: ACM Transactions on Computer-Human Interaction 29(4), Article 38

review.locator: Section 5.1 (participants, pre-processing) and results on individual fastest/slowest/preferred fonts
review.notes: DOI resolves to the ACM DL (HTTP 403 to automated fetch); Crossref abstract and author PDF (https://jeffhuang.com/papers/Readability_TOCHI22.pdf) read. Confirmed: 500 recruited on Mechanical Turk, 352 retained; 16 fonts perceptually normalised to Times at 16px; five fonts per participant; 314 / 232 / 275 WPM for fastest / slowest / preferred font; 35% fastest-vs-slowest; preferred font was fastest 20% of the time and slowest 20% of the time (chance among five).

sources.title: Impact of Font Style on Reading Parameters: Comparing Radner Reading Charts Printed in Times New Roman and Arial
sources.venue: Ophthalmic and Physiological Optics (journal title as given in Crossref metadata)

review.notes: Springer landing page redirected to a login for automated fetch; abstract and licence obtained from Crossref (publisher-deposited). Confirmed: online 27 Oct 2026; 63 native German speakers (mean age 42.4); ISO 7921:2024 RADNER charts printed in Times New Roman PS and Arial MS, x-heights equalised, 40 cm; no significant differences for any acuity or reading-speed parameter (all p > 0.40 for reading speed). NOT CONFIRMED: the specific estimate 0.124 WPM, 95% CI -1.980 to 2.246, p=.91 (from the synthesis; consistent with the abstract but not shown in it). The journal name in Crossref looks inconsistent with the Springer DOI prefix; not resolved.

sources.title: Personalized Font Recommendations: Combining ML and Typographic Guidelines to Optimize Readability

review.notes: DOI identified via Crossref. Adobe Research landing page fetched 2026-11-12. Confirmed: 252 crowdsourced participants; eight fonts; FontMART learning-to-rank model; predicted fastest font gives an average 14-25 WPM over other font defaults without reported comprehension loss. NOT CONFIRMED: 16px size, the specific 14.4 WPM (vs Georgia) and 14.8 WPM (vs Arial) gains, and the statement that apparent size was not equalised — these come from the synthesis only.

sources.title: Smaller visual angles show greater benefit of letter boldness than larger visual angles

review.notes: Author PDF (https://typ.dk/wp-content/uploads/2023/07/2019ActaPsych-BeierOderkerk.pdf) read. Confirmed: two single-letter recognition experiments with 21 and 15 participants (the 'samples of 21 and 15' in the synthesis); very thin and extremely bold weights reduced recognition at all tested sizes; a boldness benefit appeared at small but not large visual angles. Open access under CC BY-NC-ND 4.0.

sources.title: The effect of font width on eye movements during reading

review.notes: Not linked in the synthesis; identified via Crossref; abstract read via Europe PMC (PMID 34225106). Confirmed: n=25; four Univers widths; Ultra Condensed changed eye movements (fewer fixations and saccades, longer fixations) but no reading-speed differences. NOT CONFIRMED: the synthesis statement that comprehension did not differ (not in abstract). Crossref lists a CC BY-NC-ND licence among its licence URLs, but open access was not confirmed on the article itself, so it is kept as link-only.

sources.title: Extra-large letter spacing improves reading in dyslexia
sources.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 109(28):11455-11459

review.notes: PMC3396504 fetched 2026-11-12. Confirmed: follow-up with 20 Italian children with dyslexia, oral reading of text printed on A4 paper, line spacing of normal text doubled to match the spaced text; session 1: 1.87 vs 1.64 syllables/s (t(19)=2.16, p<.05), errors 6 vs 11.8 (t(19)=4.22, p<.001); session 2 (reversed assignment): 2.07 vs 1.72 syll/s (p<.005), errors 4.95 vs 13.5 (p<.001). Main experiment: 74 children (34 Italian, 40 French). Published under the PNAS open access option; specific licence not stated on the page.

sources.title: Inter-letter spacing, inter-word spacing, and font with dyslexia-friendly features: testing text readability in people with and without dyslexia

review.notes: Full text read via Europe PMC (PMC7188700, CC BY). Confirmed: 128 native-Italian children (64 with dyslexia, 64 age-matched controls, mean age 12.4) reading 8 texts aloud; default spacing 4.10 syll/s (SD 1.19), increased inter-letter spacing only 3.96 (SD 1.25), t(127)=-4.803, Bonferroni p<.001, d=-0.424; increased letter + word spacing 4.11 (SD 1.21); no effect of dyslexia-friendly letterforms.

sources.title: Dyslexie font does not benefit reading in children with or without dyslexia

review.notes: Full text read via Europe PMC (PMC5934461, CC BY). Confirmed: Experiment 1, 170 Dutch children with dyslexia, text reading, Dyslexie not faster or more accurate than Arial, most preferred Arial, preference unrelated to performance. CLARIFICATION: the synthesis's 'second sample of 147 children' consisted of 102 children with dyslexia and 45 without, reading word lists in Dyslexie, Arial and Times New Roman.

sources.title: Shorter Lines Facilitate Reading in Those Who Struggle

review.locator: Methods (procedure, data exclusion) and Results (RATE measure)
review.notes: Full text read via Europe PMC (PMC3734020). Confirmed: 27 students with dyslexia (one lost in analysis); instantaneous reading rate (RATE, gaze-derived) 27% faster in the small-device (POD) condition than the larger-device (PAD) condition; fixations -11%; regressive saccades more than halved; 208-word passage needed 12 page turns on POD vs 1 on PAD; ceiling effect in comprehension handled separately. Licence per Crossref/Europe PMC: CC0 1.0 public-domain dedication (not CC BY).

sources.title: How bold can we be? The impact of adjusting font grade on readability in light and dark polarities
sources.venue: Proceedings of the 2023 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI '23), pp. 1-11

review.locator: Section 3.2 (paragraph study method, data cleaning), 4.2 (Android paragraph results), preference results
review.notes: Full text read from https://thereadabilityconsortium.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/07/How-bold-can-we-be-The-impact-of-adjusting-font-grade-on-readability-in-light-and-dark-polarities-1.pdf; DOI taken from the PDF's citation block and confirmed via Crossref, which also lists a CC BY 4.0 licence. Confirmed: 459 participants across two studies; paragraph study screened in 410 US adults on Android phones, 333 retained; Roboto Flex 14px, weight 400, 0.25px letter spacing, #121212 / #FFFFFF; repeated-measures ANOVA effect of mode F=12.8, p<0.01, partial eta^2=0.038; light mode more readable t(332)=3.5. Preference split as extracted from the PDF: light 34%, dark 36%, switch modes 25% (the synthesis rounds this to thirds with 'either').

sources.title: Positive display polarity is advantageous for both younger and older adults

review.notes: Full text read from the university-hosted PDF linked by the synthesis. Confirmed: 169 participants (85 older, 84 younger), native German speakers; 250-word texts in 10pt Helvetica at 50 cm; polarity effect on error detection F(1,165)=9.92, p<.01, eta^2=.06; reading rate F(1,165)=0.16, p=.69.

sources.title: Positive display polarity is particularly advantageous for small character sizes: Implications for display design

review.notes: The synthesis links an in-press author manuscript (HHU); that manuscript was read, and the published abstract was checked via Europe PMC (PMID 25141597). DOI from Crossref. Confirmed: 160 participants (78 positive, 82 negative polarity); proofreading at 8/10/12/14 pt; positive-polarity advantage grows as characters get smaller; glare rating 1.97 vs 1.68 on a 1-4 scale, t(157)=2.00, p=.024, d=0.32. OMISSION IN THE SYNTHESIS: the same table shows more perceived blur with dark (negative) polarity, 2.08 vs 1.44, t(155)=-5.31, p<.001, d=-0.74, and more difficulty jumping to the next line, 1.65 vs 1.47, p=.048. Observation: t=2.00 with df=157 corresponds to a two-sided p of about .047, so the reported p-values appear one-sided (not stated in the extracted table). Numbers come from the accepted manuscript, not the version of record.

sources.title: Good Background Colors for Readers: A Study of People with and without Dyslexia
sources.venue: ASSETS '17: Proceedings of the 19th International ACM SIGACCESS Conference on Computers and Accessibility, pp. 72-80

review.notes: Author PDF (https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~jbigham/pubs/pdfs/2017/colors.pdf) read; DOI from the PDF. Confirmed: 341 participants (89 with dyslexia), native Spanish speakers; ten background colours (Blue, Blue Grey, Green, Grey, Orange, Peach, Purple, Red, Turquoise, Yellow) with black 18-point Arial, left-justified; measures were reading time and mouse distance, with comprehension questions used as a validity filter; warm colours (Peach, Orange, Yellow) gave better performance than cool colours (Blue, Blue Grey, Green); white/off-white named only as future work.

sources.title: Psychophysics of reading. VI — The role of contrast in low vision

review.notes: The author-hosted PDF linked by the synthesis returned HTTP 403. DOI via Crossref; abstract read via Europe PMC (PMID 2788957). Confirmed: 19 low-vision observers; 6-degree letters; five read white-on-black faster than black-on-white at high and low contrast; four of those five had cloudy ocular media; critical contrast higher than normal in 16 of 19 (average 3.9x).

sources.title: Column setting and text justification influence return-sweep eye movement behavior during Chinese multi-line reading

review.locator: Participants; return-sweep results (corrective saccades); comprehension questions
review.notes: Full text read via Europe PMC (PMC11147972, CC BY). Confirmed: 44 students (Tianjin Normal University); single vs double column and left- vs fully-justified Chinese text; corrective saccades 45% (single) vs 33% (double); 40% (left-justified) vs 38% (fully justified); minimal influence on overall reading time; comprehension checked with three yes/no literal questions per text. The exact p-value for the column effect was not located in the extracted text.

sources.title: Applying Writing Guidelines to Web Pages

review.notes: Fetched 2026-11-12. Confirmed: 21 technical users, between-subjects comparison of an original site and a rewritten site; 159% overall usability improvement (geometric mean of task time 80%, task errors 809%, memory 100%, satisfaction 37%); the rewrite combined concise text (54% of original length), scannable layout (summaries, bullets, highlighted keywords, more headings, shorter paragraphs) and objective language. No typography-only condition.

sources.title: Is it the size, the movement, or both? Investigating effects of screen size and text movement on processing, understanding, and motivation when students read informational text

review.notes: Abstract and licence obtained from Crossref (publisher-deposited). Confirmed: Norwegian university students; smartphone vs tablet x scrolling vs paging; paging tended to give better integrated understanding and more strategic backtracking; tablet scrolling gave a more positive reading experience. NOT CONFIRMED: n=145 and the scores 9.06 vs 7.86 (p=.066) — from the synthesis only. Online 27 Aug 2022, issue Sept 2023.

sources.title: Scrolling and hyperlinks: The effects of two prevalent digital features on children's digital reading comprehension

review.notes: Abstract and licence obtained from Crossref. Confirmed: 75 English-speaking children in Grades 3-5 (mean 9.9 years), online, within-participants; Gates-MacGinitie passages; comprehension higher with no digital features (clicking) than with hover-definition hyperlinks; clicking and scrolling similar. NOT CONFIRMED: 74% vs 67%, p=.007, d=.30 — from the synthesis only.

sources.title: Evaluating Interactive Highlighting Techniques in Digital Reading: An Empirical Study of Hover-Based Line, Sentence, and Paragraph Highlighting

review.notes: Fetched https://www.journals.uc.edu/index.php/vl/article/view/8818 on 2026-11-12 (DOI shown there and confirmed via Crossref). Confirmed: 80 participants; hover-based line, sentence and paragraph highlighting vs static text; no significant reading-speed or comprehension differences; perceived attention higher for sentence- and paragraph-level highlighting than static. NOT CONFIRMED: laptop, 16px, 1.5 line height and 70-80 CPL (from the synthesis only).

sources.title: An Eye-Tracking Study on Text Accessibility and Comprehension in University Students

review.notes: Full text read via Europe PMC (PMC13296324, CC BY). Confirmed: 24 young adults without cognitive disabilities; hard-to-read, control and Easy-to-Read (E2R) formats, all with 1.5 line spacing and font size 18 (unit as reported); E2R above hard-to-read for comprehension; E2R vs control only a trend after Bonferroni correction (log-odds -0.288, adjusted 95% CI -0.597 to 0.021, OR 0.75, p=0.077); viewing distance 98 cm. Bibliographic data (Behavioral Sciences 16(6):1041, 22 June 2026) confirmed via Crossref.

sources.title: To boldly go where no text has gone before: The effects of boldface letters on eye movements in reading

review.notes: Abstract read via Europe PMC (PMID 40240742). Confirmed: tested Bionic Reading-style bolding of the first half of words against bolding the middle or last half and against unbolded text; first-half bolding did not help and produced costs relative to unbolded reading; no subgroup benefit found. NOT CONFIRMED: that the study was preregistered (not stated in the abstract).

sources.title: A reliable and valid questionnaire was developed to measure computer vision syndrome at the workplace

review.notes: Abstract read via Europe PMC (PMID 25744132; the synthesis linked the PubMed record). Confirmed: CVS-Q designed and validated for computer workers at the workplace; 16 symptoms rated for frequency and intensity; Rasch analysis; sensitivity and specificity above 70%; test-retest ICC 0.802.

limitations: No factorial or confirmatory experiment has tested this combination as a whole.
Nominal px and CPL values do not fix apparent size; x-height, viewing distance and rendering change what the reader actually sees.
Meeting 7:1 for body text satisfies the ordinary-text threshold of SC 1.4.6 only; it does not make a page AAA conformant.
A 1.5 line height on its own does not satisfy every part of SC 1.4.8 Visual Presentation.

claims.title: Practical desktop baseline: ~65 CPL, 18px, 1.5 line height, regular weight, default spacing, at least 7:1
claims.statement: For Latin-script continuous prose on desktop, a defensible starting configuration is roughly 65 characters per line, 18px nominal body size, line height 1.5, a regular or book weight, the typeface's own letter and word spacing, and body-text contrast of at least 7:1, together with reader controls for size, spacing, width, font and colours. This is a product design choice. No experiment has tested this exact package or shown that it maximises reading speed, comprehension or comfort.

claims.title: Larger-text hypothesis: 60 CPL, 20px, line height 1.6
claims.statement: A candidate 'reading-optimised' configuration is 60 CPL, 20px body text, line height 1.6 (32px baseline distance) and a 15px extra paragraph gap, keeping the same face, spacing, colours and accessibility features as the baseline. Because each character is larger, fewer characters per line does not mean a physically narrower column: with the same face, 60 characters at 20px span roughly as much width as 65 characters at 18px (60 x 20 = 1200 vs 65 x 18 = 1170 size-units). Expected costs are more vertical space and more scrolling or paging. For a speed, comprehension or eye-strain advantage of this configuration over the baseline: No reliable quantitative improvement established.
claims.plain: Slightly bigger text with a bit more space between lines is an idea worth testing. Nobody has shown yet that it works better.

claims.title: Sample-size planning: ~90 participants for d=0.30, ~200 for d=0.20 (paired)
claims.statement: For a single paired comparison at 80% power and two-sided alpha .05, about 90 complete participants detect a standardised within-person difference of 0.30 and about 200 detect 0.20. These figures do not power a full width-by-height factorial, subgroup analyses or a tight comprehension non-inferiority margin. A 24–30-person pilot to estimate variance, followed by simulation, with an initial budget envelope of 150–250 participants, is a reasonable plan. Success thresholds such as a speed gain of at least 5% with a CI excluding zero and a comprehension lower bound above −3 percentage points are product choices, not established minimums.
claims.plain: Studies need enough people to detect small differences; a few dozen is only enough for a first try.

claims.title: Viewing distance, luminance, ambient light, glare and visual needs cannot be inferred from page styles
claims.statement: A page's CSS reveals nominal sizes, colours and spacing, but not the reader's viewing distance, display luminance, ambient lighting, glare, display scaling or visual abilities. These determine apparent size and comfort and must be measured, recorded or asked about rather than assumed from styles.
claims.plain: The page's code can't tell how far you sit from the screen, how bright it is, or how well you see.

gaps.description: The full report (Digital_Reading_Typography_Evidence_Report.docx, 44 references) was not available; only a summary with about 30 linked sources was. Roughly 14 references, and the report's detailed study assessments, tables and numerical specifications, are unknown and unextracted.

Dyson & Haselgrove (2001) could not be verified: the publisher page was inaccessible and the synthesis's link for it actually points to Dyson & Kipping (1998). Sample size, comprehension result and p-value remain secondary.
The October 2026 study of partial-word bolding with English-as-a-foreign-language readers (reported by the synthesis at abstract level) could not be identified; no link or citation was given.

Numbers taken from the synthesis but not confirmed in the parts of the originals that were accessible: Rudnay 2026 (0.124 WPM, 95% CI -1.980 to 2.246, p=.91); Cai 2022 (14.4 / 14.8 WPM vs Georgia / Arial, 16px, unequalised apparent size); Haverkamp (n=145, 9.06 vs 7.86, p=.066); Krenca (74% vs 67%, p=.007, d=.30); Vatány (laptop, 16px, 1.5, 70-80 CPL); Dyson & Kipping (n=48 and 24); Minakata & Beier (no comprehension difference); Spear 2025 (preregistration).
Bernard et al. is dated 2003 in the synthesis, but the linked article is Usability News 4.2 (July 2002). A possible 2003 conference version was not located or checked.

Script and language coverage: apart from one Chinese study (Wang et al. 2024), the synthesis covers Latin-script (mostly English, German, Italian, Dutch, Spanish, Norwegian) research only. No evidence was extracted for Japanese or Korean, right-to-left scripts (Arabic, Hebrew, Persian, Urdu), Indic or other complex scripts, or languages with special casing and diacritic needs such as Turkish (dotted/dotless i). WCAG's 40-glyph CJK width limit is normative, not empirical.

No extracted study measures comfort, fatigue or place loss over sustained 20-30 minute reading sessions; nearly all experiments use short passages. The synthesis proposes such sessions but cites no results.

Evidence on how a contrast ratio between 4.5:1 and 21:1 affects speed, comprehension or comfort for normally sighted adults on modern displays, separated from absolute luminance, was not found in the synthesis.
Older readers, low-vision readers, readers with attention-related difficulties and adult readers with dyslexia are thinly covered; most dyslexia evidence is from children reading aloud.

Some originals were only partly accessible to automated verification: author-hosted PDFs for Legge & Bigelow (2011) and Rubin & Legge (1989) returned HTTP 403 (verified via abstracts only); the Piepenbrock 2014 numbers come from the accepted manuscript, not the version of record; the Shaikh & Chaparro HFES paper was checked at abstract level, with numbers taken from the companion Usability News article.

Results reported in the originals but omitted by the synthesis were added during verification (Rello 2016 comprehension effects of line spacing and font size; Piepenbrock 2014 blur and line-jump ratings). Other originals that were checked only at abstract level may contain further omitted results.
